A balance-transfer promotion has a deadline, a fee and a remaining balance

Four graphics compare promotional and later rates, debt paths, full repayment charges and the payment needed to finish during the promotion.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 4 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Explore a promotional balance-transfer schedule

Interactive planning lab

Months to repay the transferred balance28

Hypothetical single transferred balance with no new purchases or other rate buckets. Fee is financed into the balance and receives the same modeled rate. Rates are nominal annual divided by 12; interest is charged before each fixed month-end payment. The within-promotion payment is rounded up to cents, with the final payment capped at debt owed. Promotional rate applies to the first selected monthly cycles, then the follow-on rate applies prospectively to remaining debt. No retroactive interest, late payment, promotion cancellation, annual fee, contractual minimum formula or actual issuer allocation rule is calculated. Both alternatives stop at payoff or 120 months; incomplete interest is partial. These are assumptions, not available card offers.

The central idea

A low starting rate is one input. Include the transfer fee, the amount left when the promotion ends and the payment schedule before comparing borrowing costs.

01

Read what the offer applies to and when it ends

The FCAC’s credit-card guide explains balance-transfer fees and promotions that apply for a specified period. It also distinguishes purchase grace periods from balance transfers, which do not receive that purchase grace period.

This model isolates one transferred debt. There are no new purchases, cash advances or competing rate buckets. The transfer fee is added to the opening balance and receives the same modeled rate. An actual agreement can treat fees and payments differently.

The promotional rate applies for a selected number of monthly cycles. The follow-on rate then applies to remaining debt prospectively. The model includes neither retroactive interest nor the consequences of losing a promotion through a missed payment. All rates and terms are hypothetical.

02

Include the fee in the amount that needs repayment

The default current balance is CAD 10,000 at a 20% nominal annual rate. A transfer fee of 3% adds CAD 300, so the alternative starts with CAD 10,300 of debt. A zero promotional rate does not remove that fee.

The selected payment is CAD 400 at each month-end. With twelve promotional cycles at 0%, those payments reduce the transferred balance by CAD 4,800. CAD 5,500 therefore remains when the promotion ends.

From the next cycle, the example charges a 22% nominal annual rate divided by twelve on remaining debt before the payment. Actual cards can calculate daily interest and use different payment allocation rules. The illustration uses one explicit monthly convention so the schedule can be inspected.

03

Solve the payment needed to clear during the promotion

The second metric calculates a constant monthly amount that would repay the fee-inclusive balance within the promotional cycles. At 0%, CAD 10,300 divided by twelve is CAD 858.333… per month. The tool rounds up to CAD 858.34, with the final payment capped at the remaining amount. Rounding down to CAD 858.33 would leave four cents after twelve payments.

That amount is more than the selected CAD 400 payment. The difference explains why the default schedule continues beyond the promotion. At a positive promotional rate, the tool uses the fixed-payment amortization formula rather than simply dividing principal by months.

If zero promotional cycles are selected, the new balance begins at the follow-on rate and no within-promotion payment is reported. A zero original debt creates no transfer fee in the model. The metric does not determine affordability or replace actual minimum-payment requirements.

04

Compare the complete schedule when it is available

Under the defaults, the current balance clears in month thirty-three and incurs approximately CAD 3,044.21 of interest. The transferred balance clears in month twenty-eight, with approximately CAD 895.35 of interest and the CAD 300 fee.

The transfer’s modeled borrowing cost is therefore CAD 1,195.35, about CAD 1,848.86 below the current-card cost under these assumptions. Original principal is excluded from both cost bars because it must be repaid either way. Interest on the financed fee is already included in the interest component.

The charts stop at payoff or 120 months. A “Not repaid” metric means the model did not clear that balance within the limit. Charges for an incomplete schedule are partial and cannot be called a full repayment cost. The matrix uses NR instead of reporting a full-life cost for such cases.

05

Test the payment and the time available

The matrix changes monthly payments and promotional cycles while holding the original balance, fee and rates fixed. Each completed cell shows total interest plus the fee. A larger promotional window helps only within the entered repayment schedule and assumptions.

The comparison keeps the same fixed payment while each balance remains outstanding. It does not invest money released after earlier payoff, add an annual card fee or simulate new spending. Those effects belong in a wider household comparison if they apply.

The FCAC notes that missed payments can cause the loss of promotional terms. Check the agreement, transaction types, fee treatment, minimum payments and expiry dates before relying on an actual offer. The four graphics explain a cost schedule without treating a headline rate as a complete borrowing decision.

Original scenario calculations and research checklists are TickerLantern’s educational analysis; attributed publisher examples retain their stated source and scope.
